UPI Consolidated Circular v1.0 (NPCI/UPI/CC/01, 18 Sep 2026) consolidates UPI Operating Circulars up to 31 July 2026 and withdraws those in Annexure G (secondary).
Under CC/01, UPI IDs/Numbers inactive for one year are disabled and revised merchant QR requirements apply to QRs issued or replaced from 1 Dec 2026 (secondary).
CC/01 likely subsumes OC-215A, OC-220 and other standalone circulars; needs verification against Annexure G.
From 1 Oct 2025 PSPs must ensure no P2P collect request is initiated, routed or processed (UPI-OC-No-220-FY-2025-26, secondary).
P2P collect had been capped at ₹2,000 since 2019 (Circular 76); for small/non-verified (P2PM) merchants collect and share-intent/QR share-and-pay are restricted to ₹2,000 (secondary).
With P2P collect discontinued, P2P on UPI is push-only; merchant (P2M) collect is not stated as discontinued.

UPI-OC-215A caps balance enquiry at 50 per app per customer per 24 hours (customer-initiated only) and list-account at 25 per app per customer per day; AutoPay executions only in non-peak hours with one attempt plus three retries; peak hours 10:00 to 13:00 and 17:00 to 21:30 (secondary).
OC-215A compliance deadlines: members to communicate compliance by 31 July 2025, PSP API queueing and acquirer audits by 31 Aug 2025; the 1 Aug 2025 effective date is from secondary reporting.
A 26 Apr 2025 NPCI circular says the first UPI status check may only be made 90 seconds after the original transaction (secondary).

From 15 Sep 2025 specified verified P2M categories can transact up to ₹5 lakh per transaction and ₹10 lakh per 24 hours; credit card bill payments ₹5 lakh per transaction, ₹6 lakh per day; P2P unchanged at ₹1 lakh per day (secondary, public broadcaster).
NPCI index lists OC 127 and OC 185 (₹5 lakh per transaction for specific categories), OC76A (limits by merchant and transaction type) and OC 192 (maximum inward credit limits for P2PM merchants).
Device-native face/fingerprint authentication was reported live 8 Oct 2025 as an optional alternative to the UPI PIN, on-device, initially up to ₹5,000, disabled on rooted devices (secondary).
RBI Authentication Directions permit device-native and Aadhaar-based biometrics as factors and exempt UPI tap-and-pay on NFC POS from the two-factor rule.
NPCI index lists OC 116 (Aadhaar OTP authentication in lieu of debit card for UPI onboarding) and OC 137 (revised timeline).
TPAPs are limited to 30% of total UPI volume, bank apps exempt; introduced November 2020; deadline extended on 31 Dec 2024 by two years to 31 December 2026 (secondary).
NPCI index lists an SOP: Market Share Cap for TPAP; no 2026 decision found before search budget ran out.

UPI Lite is an on-device LITE balance for low-value payments, described as below ₹500 per transaction, working without real-time use of remitter bank CBS; balance not carried to a new device and refunded to bank account after checks.
Widely reported higher UPI Lite limits than the NPCI page's below-₹500 description were not verified.
NPCI index lists OC 138 (introduction of on-device wallet UPI Lite) and OC 179 (Lite top-up).
UPI 123PAY offers four feature-phone channels: IVR, missed call, native feature-phone app (incl. camera scan and pay) and proximity sound via merchant sound box; no limits or launch date on the page.
NPCI index lists RuPay OC022, FY 23-24: transaction limit for linked RuPay credit card on UPI; CC/01 covers RuPay credit card on UPI and credit line/PPI on UPI.

NPCI dispute circulars include Circular 98 (UDIR complaint handling), OC 106 (UDIR auto reversal for deemed approved cases marked RET), OC 145 (ODR final timeline) and Circular 17 (debit reversals and deemed-approved reconciliation); dates not shown.

Under RBI's TAT framework (RBI/2019-20/67), a UPI debit without beneficiary credit must be reversed by the beneficiary bank by T+1, else ₹100 per day; a UPI P2M debit without merchant confirmation must be auto-reversed by T+5, else ₹100 per day; compensation is automatic; T is the calendar day.

UPI-PayNow has been operational since Feb 2023; UPI QR acceptance is live in Bhutan, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Qatar, Singapore, Sri Lanka and UAE; UPI-like infrastructure is ongoing in Namibia and Peru; Project Nexus is ongoing.

UPI-PayNow limit is ₹60,000 per day (about SGD 1,000), P2P only for maintenance of relatives and gifts, with LRS limits applying outward; Indian receiving banks Axis, DBS India, ICICI, Indian Bank, IOB, SBI; sending ICICI, Indian Bank, IOB, SBI; Singapore DBS and Liquid Group.
A bank blog says UPI remains free for consumers and any MDR framework is prospective, citing no circular.
NPCI ranks MCCs by UPI volume with 5411 groceries, 5814 fast food and 5812 restaurants in the top tier (Sep 2024 classification); statistics page not opened directly.
UPI settlement asset is very likely central bank money (member settlement accounts at RBI) but no opened primary source states it.

RTGS settles continuously transaction by transaction without netting in RBI's books, so payments are final and irrevocable; 24x7x365 since 14 Dec 2020; minimum ₹2 lakh, no maximum; beneficiary credit within 30 minutes.

RTGS returns within one hour or before end of the RTGS business day, delays compensated at repo plus 2%; 22-character UTR; credit-push only; outward charges capped at ₹25 (₹2 to 5 lakh) and ₹50 (above ₹5 lakh).
NGRTGS was upgraded from v3.0 to v4.0 in 2025-26; RTGS handled 3,500 lakh transactions worth ₹2,273.7 lakh crore.

NEFT runs half-hourly batches around the clock every day; the RBI-operated NEFT Processing Centre sorts by beneficiary bank and books entries; credit within two hours of batch settlement or return in the same window; penal interest repo plus 2% automatically; no RBI amount limit; savings account online NEFT free since 1 Jan 2020.

NEFT has been ISO 20022 compliant since 2023 (230+ banks used a converter); in 2025-26 all member banks migrated to send ISO messages directly; NEFT handled 1,00,996 lakh transactions worth ₹502.3 lakh crore.
NEFT as deferred net settlement in RBI books is an inference from batch processing; 48 batches is arithmetic, not stated.
CTS continuous clearing phase 1 went live 4 Oct 2025, cutting clearing from T+1 to a few hours with credit within one hour of settlement.

IMPS offers instant 24x7x365 interbank transfers using mobile + 7-digit MMID or account + IFSC across mobile, internet, branch, ATM and SMS; eligible members hold an RBI banking or PPI licence; 867 live members; pilot Aug 2010, public launch 22 Nov 2010.
IMPS 2025-26 volume fell to 49,431 lakh from 56,250 lakh while value rose to ₹76.7 lakh crore.
NACH handles bulk credits (subsidy, dividend, salary, pension) and debits (utilities, loans, MF, insurance) with a Mandate Management System; APBS routes Aadhaar-linked government benefits.
NACH credits were 18,284 lakh (₹19.0 lakh crore) and debits 21,614 lakh (₹26.9 lakh crore) in 2025-26.

The E-mandate Framework 2026 covers recurring payments via cards, PPI and UPI (domestic and cross-border); AFA-free up to ₹15,000 per transaction and ₹1,00,000 for insurance premiums, MF subscriptions and credit card bills; pre-debit notice at least 24 hours before (not FASTag/NCMC auto-replenish); registration, modification, withdrawal and opt-out need AFA; replaces eight circulars from 21 Aug 2019 to 22 Aug 2024.
AePS supports cash withdrawal, deposit, balance, mini statement and Aadhaar-to-Aadhaar transfer at any bank's BC micro-ATM using UIDAI biometric authentication.
In 2025-26 RBI issued directions to streamline onboarding of AePS touchpoint operators and strengthen acquiring-bank risk management.
BBPS has 10 authorised BBPOUs and 1 BBPCU; all 10 BBPOUs were inspected in 2025-26.
BBPS rename to Bharat Connect not confirmed from primary source (page blocked).
RuPay stack deployment for domestic card schemes is complete in Mauritius and UAE.
Small PPIs (with or without cash loading) cap outstanding at ₹10,000, loading ₹10,000/month and ₹1,20,000/year, no cash-out or transfers, and must convert to full-KYC within 24 months.

Full-KYC PPIs allow up to ₹2,00,000 outstanding, transfers ₹10,000/month or up to ₹2,00,000/month per pre-registered beneficiary, cash withdrawal ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000/month; gift PPI ₹10,000; PPI-MTS ₹3,000.

Interoperability is mandatory for full-KYC PPIs (wallets via UPI, cards via authorised networks); non-banks need a sponsor bank for UPI settlement; non-bank balances held in escrow at a scheduled commercial bank; non-bank net worth ₹5 crore at application, ₹15 crore within three FYs.
There were 50 non-bank and 63 bank PPI issuers at end-March 2026.

PA Directions 2025 define PA-P, PA-O and PA-CB; banks need no authorisation; non-banks must be authorised Indian companies with net worth ₹15 crore at application and ₹25 crore by end of third FY; merchant funds in escrow at a scheduled commercial bank (PA-CB uses InCA/OCA at AD Cat-I banks).

PA settlement to merchants has no RBI-fixed T+ days (per PA-merchant agreement); merchant CDD per KYC MD with CKYCR retrieval, simplified up to ₹40 lakh turnover; non-bank PAs register with FIU-IND; PA-CB max ₹25 lakh per transaction with no co-mingling or netting; card credentials not stored on merchant-accessed systems.

PA Directions repeal the PA/PG guidelines of 17 Mar 2020 and 31 Mar 2021 and the PA-CB circular of 31 Oct 2023; PA-P-only entities apply by 31 Dec 2025 or wind up by 28 Feb 2026; new merchant onboarding rules from 1 Jan 2026.
Authorised non-bank PAs rose from 51 to 68 by end-March 2026.

Tokenisation and de-tokenisation are done only by an authorised card network or issuer (TSP); the token requestor cannot store PAN; registration requires explicit AFA consent; token tied to card, requestor and device; no cap on number of cards; tokenisation optional for customers.

From 1 Apr 2026 all digital payments need at least two distinct factors, at least one dynamic for non card-present; risk-based additional checks allowed with DigiLocker suggested for high-risk confirmations; issuers must compensate fully without demur for losses from non-compliant transactions.
Card issuers must validate non-recurring cross-border CNP AFA when the overseas merchant or acquirer requests and run risk-based checks on all cross-border CNP by 1 Oct 2026.
The PSO Authorisation MD (15 Jun 2026) states no person can operate a payment system without RBI authorisation, defines net worth and replaces six earlier circulars.

Payments Vision 2028 (27 Mar 2026, to Dec 2028) includes shared liability between remitter and beneficiary banks, per-mode enable/disable controls, a Cyber KRI framework for non-bank PSOs, e-cheques, uniform Domestic LEI and a perpetual sandbox.
The 2026-27 agenda includes exploring APP-fraud frictions, a kill switch, direct RTGS/NEFT access for more entity types, e-Kuber 3.0 and a Global SFMS Hub with UAE interlinking (planned, not rules).
The DPIP smart registry has been operational since Aug 2025 with an AI/ML risk scoring phase expected in 2026-27.
MuleHunter.ai was in 26 banks by 31 Mar 2026.

Customer financial information accessed by an AA must not reside with the AA; AAs must not request or store customer credentials; the consent artefact includes customer identity, nature of information, purpose, recipients, notification URL, creation and expiry dates, AA identity and signature; NOF at least ₹2 crore; ReBIT APIs to be adopted.
AA FI Schema 2.0 was released 23 Jan 2025 (adds account type, currency, CKYC status; mandatory vs optional fields); RBI plans to publish AA customer protection standards in 2026-27.
As of June 2026: 17 operational AAs, 2 certifiers, 176 FIPs, 1,076 FIUs, 1,117 entities live; 2,880m+ accounts enabled, 1,970m+ consents raised, 493m+ fulfilled, 295m+ monthly data shares.

Digital Lending Directions 2025 (8 May 2025) apply to commercial banks, co-operative banks, NBFCs incl. HFCs and AIFIs; effective immediately except DLA reporting on CIMS by 15 Jun 2025 and multi-lender arrangements from 1 Nov 2025.

Digital lending: disbursal to borrower's own account, repayment directly to RE account, no pass-through or pool accounts or LSP control of flows; KFS with APR; Board-set cooling-off of at least one day with exit by repaying principal plus proportionate APR.

DLG total cover is capped at 5% of the portfolio amount disbursed, only as cash, lien-marked FD at an SCB or bank guarantee, only by LSP or RE-as-LSP incorporated under the Companies Act, not for credit cards or revolving credit, invoked within 120 days overdue.

Multi-lender LSPs must show all matching offers with lender name, amount, tenor, APR, EMI, penal charges and KFS link and name non-matching lenders, with no dark patterns; all DLA lending reported to CICs; data on servers in India; overseas processing data deleted and repatriated within 24 hours; no biometric storage unless statutorily allowed; escalation to RB-IOS after 30 days.
The Digital Lending Directions repealed the 24 Jun 2020, 2 Sep 2022 and 8 Jun 2023 (DLG) instruments; whether they were re-housed in the Nov 2025 entity-wise directions needs verification.
RBI is operationalising a public directory of DLAs.
Credit Information Reporting Directions for commercial banks dated 28 Nov 2025, updated 1 Jul 2026, are listed (text not opened).

DICGC covers ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank in the same right and capacity (2.4 times GDP per capita 2025-26); at 30 Sep 2025, 291.4 crore accounts (97.5%) were fully insured and insured deposits were 41.1% of assessable; reserve ratio 2.37%.

DICGC premium was a flat 12 paise per ₹100 in 2025-26; a risk-based premium framework is effective 1 Apr 2026; 1,950 insured banks at 31 Mar 2026; claims ₹1,988 crore for 72 UCBs; DIF ₹2,61,823 crore.
The DICGC site lists the RBP press release (06.02.26), FAQs (01.04.2026) and recent s.18A payments (e.g. 9 Oct 2026) and announces no higher cover.
A Finance Ministry proposal to raise cover to ₹7.5 lakh is reported pending PMO approval; cover was last raised in Feb 2020 from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh (secondary; proposed only).
KYC Directions CB 2025 rest on PMLA 2002 and PML Rules 2005, also BR Act, PSS Act and FEMA; biometric e-KYC by bank official, BC or BF incl. Aadhaar Face Authentication.

OTP non-face-to-face e-KYC accounts: aggregate balance up to ₹1 lakh, credits up to ₹2 lakh per FY, only term loans up to ₹60,000 per year, full CDD within one year else deposit account closed; alerts only to Aadhaar-registered mobile; flagged on CKYCR upload.

V-CIP must run on the bank's own premises/secure network with end-to-end encryption, foreign/spoofed IP blocking, live GPS geo-tag and timestamp, liveness and face match, trained officials, rejection if customer is prompted, recordings stored in India and not retained by cloud providers, concurrent audit before activation and VAPT by CERT-In empanelled auditors.

CKYCR upload within 10 days of an account-based relationship and updates within 7 days; periodic updation every 2/8/10 years (high/medium/low risk); small accounts capped at ₹1 lakh credits/year, ₹10,000 withdrawals/month and ₹50,000 balance; records kept at least five years; STR to FIU-IND where CDD would tip off.

CKYCR is the first reference point; the 2026-27 agenda includes a customer identification confidence level framework and V-CIP for NRIs offshore; the KYC FAQs of 9 Jun 2025 were subsumed into KYC Directions 2025.
RBI relays UNSC list amendments to REs for action under KYC Directions chapter IX (notification of 29 Sep 2026 not reopened).

DPDP Rules 2025 were notified (PIB: 14 Nov 2025) with 18-month phased compliance; consent managers must be India-based companies; a four-member digital Data Protection Board with appeals to TDSAT; breach notice to affected individuals without delay; penalties up to ₹200 crore for breach-notice and child-data failures.

Phasing: notifications dated 13 Nov 2025; immediately in force DPB provisions and Act s.1(2), 2, 18 to 26, 35, 38 to 43, 44(1),(3) and Rules 1, 2, 17 to 21; from 12 Nov 2026 consent managers (s.6(9), 27(1)(d), Rule 4); from 12 May 2027 most obligations incl. Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22, 23 (secondary).
The DPDP Rules notification date conflicts between 13 Nov 2025 (AZB) and 14 Nov 2025 (PIB); gazette not opened.
The DPDP Act was enacted 11 Aug 2023.
Digital Banking Channels Authorisation MDs dated 28 Nov 2025 are effective 1 Jan 2026.

The PBOC carries out monetary policy under the People's Bank Law and the Commercial Bank Law; its central bank status was confirmed by the NPC on 18 March 1995; a 2003 NPCSC amendment strengthened its role (citation needed on page).
CNCC is a non-profit public institution created May 1990, administered by the PBOC, operating CNAPS components (HVPS, BEPS, IBPS, CFXPS, Check Imaging System).
The China Anti-Money Laundering Monitoring and Analysis Center sits directly under the PBOC, which also has an Anti-Money Laundering Bureau.

Under the Action Plan the PBOC sets up a Digital RMB Management Committee to coordinate functional supervision; a self-regulatory office at the DCI leads self-discipline norms; the Digital RMB Operations Management Center runs the central-bank-side system; the International Operations Center runs the cross-border system.
The plan adopts separation of regulation from operation (管办分离), with supervisory tools including data interfaces and supervisory nodes on blockchain service platforms.

NFRA was established 10 March 2023 replacing CBIRC, took over some PBOC and CSRC roles, supervises the financial sector except securities and sits under the State Council; Li Yunze became director 19 May 2023.
The NFRA page lists Li Yunze's departure on 29 April 2026 with the post vacant.

In 2023 oversight of financial holding companies and financial consumer protection moved from the PBOC to NFRA; the PBOC works under the CCP Central Financial Commission; Pan Gongsheng is governor and Party secretary (since 2023).
SAFE is the FX administrative body under PBOC management; functions include FX administration rules, BoP monitoring, FX market supervision and managing FX and gold reserves.
CAC issued Order No. 16 on cross-border data flows on 22 March 2024.
The 2025 Cybersecurity Law amendment (Art. 77) lets public security authorities and relevant departments freeze assets of, or sanction, foreign entities or individuals causing serious harm.
The China Deposit Insurance Corporation was set up in 2019 as a wholly owned PBOC subsidiary.
e-CNY Center International Co., Ltd. (Shanghai) operates CBETS under the guidance of the PBOC DCI (Xinhua English); Xinhua's Chinese report says the center was set up and managed by the DCI.

HVPS is RTGS, the backbone of the national payments system, launched June 2005; in 2023 it processed 382 million transactions worth RMB 8,481 trillion; at end-2016 it had 305 direct and 141,023 indirect participants.
BEPS is a retail bulk system embedded in HVPS with real-time netting and settlement at set intervals, launched June 2006; in 2023 it processed 4.6 billion transactions worth RMB 186 trillion.

IBPS has provided internet-based instant payments since August 2010 using deferred net settlement; in 2023 it processed 17 billion transactions worth about RMB 301 trillion; in July 2020 it had 218 direct and 175 proxy-access participants.

CFXPS is RTGS for domestic foreign-currency payments (from 2008 as CDFCPS); the Check Imaging System (2007) settles multilaterally net at HVPS; CFETS clears domestic RMB FX trades with RMB legs settled through HVPS; BOC (Hong Kong) and BOC (Macau) are HVPS direct participants and clearing agents.

CIPS direct participants fund their CIPS position from HVPS clearing accounts (message hvps.112, business type A200), confirming HVPS clearing accounts at the PBOC as the central-bank-money source for CIPS.
China UnionPay launched in Shanghai on 26 March 2002 with PBOC approval; it is the only interbank network linking all banks' ATMs nationwide and is described as state-owned.
Non-bank payment institutions must route cross-institution payments through a PBOC-designated clearing institution and may not carry out clearing themselves (Art. 30).
2020 rules required online-payment clearing to go through NetsUnion Clearing Corporation (secondary).
A 2021 MIIT mandate led to interoperable payment QR codes between Alipay, WeChat Pay and UnionPay Cloud QuickPass (secondary).

China has built a unified cross-border QR code gateway as the single interface for cross-border QR cooperation; as of end-June 2026 UnionPay, NetsUnion and other clearing institutions had QR interconnection with 13 countries including Malaysia (secondary citing PBOC report).

Cross-Border Payment Connect links mainland fast payments with other central banks' fast payment systems; mainland to Hong Kong went live June 2025 with 14 mainland and 26 Hong Kong institutions at end-June 2026; mainland to UAE opened to the public in April 2026 (secondary).
Which CNCC system is the mainland fast payment system in Cross-Border Payment Connect is not stated (IBPS is the likely candidate).
Decree 768 was adopted on 24 November 2023, published 17 December 2023 and took effect 1 May 2024.

Art. 2: a non-bank payment institution is a licensed LLC or joint-stock company, other than a bank, transferring funds on electronic payment instructions; overseas non-bank entities serving mainland users must set up a domestic institution unless otherwise provided.
Art. 15 sets two business categories, stored-value account operation and payment transaction processing, with detailed classification by the PBOC.
Art. 8: minimum registered capital RMB 100 million paid in cash, which the PBOC may raise; Arts. 6, 10, 13: the PBOC approves establishment, issues licences and approves major changes.

Arts. 27 to 29: customer reserve funds may move only on user instructions and may not be misappropriated or pledged; net assets must meet a PBOC ratio to average daily reserves; reserves are deposited at the PBOC or PBOC-approved commercial banks and protected from creditor freezing except as provided by law.

Arts. 18, 19, 33: business systems and backups must be in mainland China; domestic transactions processed, settled and stored domestically; cross-border services must comply with cross-border payment, RMB, FX and data rules.
Alipay was one of the first licensed non-financial payment institutions (2011 licence) and served over 1.3 billion users and 80 million merchants as of June 2020 (Ant Group HKEX filing, secondary).
Alipay and Tenpay let Chinese residents pay by QR in nearly 80 countries and regions and have brought more than 40 foreign wallets into China for inbound use (secondary citing PBOC report).

The historical 100% centralised deposit of reserve funds at the PBOC (Jan 2019 per common accounts) was not sourced; Decree 768 permits PBOC or approved banks, so the current arrangement needs verification.

Deposit Insurance Regulations (Decree No. 660): approved 29 Oct 2014, signed 17 Feb 2015, published 31 Mar 2015, effective 1 May 2015; Art. 5 max payout RMB 500,000 per depositor per insured institution, principal and interest combined.

Art. 2 covers deposit-taking banking institutions in mainland China, excluding overseas branches and foreign bank branches unless a treaty provides; Art. 4 excludes interbank deposits and senior managers' deposits at their own institution.
CAC Order No. 16 was adopted 28 Nov 2023 and published and effective 22 Mar 2024.

Art. 5 exempts PI transfers needed to perform contracts the individual is party to, including cross-border shopping and remittance, and non-CIIO transfers of fewer than 100,000 individuals' non-sensitive PI since 1 January of the year.

Art. 7 requires a security assessment for CIIOs, important data, 1 million or more individuals' PI or 10,000 or more individuals' sensitive PI; Art. 8 applies a standard contract or certification between 100,000 and 1 million.
Art. 6 lets FTZs adopt negative lists; Art. 9 assessments valid 3 years; Art. 13 Order No. 16 prevails over inconsistent provisions of CAC Orders No. 11 (2022) and No. 13 (2023).
The NPCSC Decision amending the Cybersecurity Law was adopted 28 Oct 2025 (14th NPCSC, 18th session) and is effective 1 Jan 2026.

The amendment adds AI governance (Art. 20), ties PI handling to the Civil Code and PIPL (Art. 42), raises fines (CII operators up to RMB 10 million for particularly severe consequences), penalises uncertified critical network equipment (Art. 63) and CII procurement without security review (Art. 67), and adds a mitigation clause (Art. 73) and foreign-actor sanctions (Art. 77).
The original Cybersecurity Law was adopted 7 Nov 2016 and took effect 1 Jun 2017 (secondary).

PIPL was adopted 20 Aug 2021 and took effect 1 Nov 2021; cross-border routes are a CAC security assessment, certification or a standard contract, plus separate consent and notice (secondary; official text not opened).
Decree 768 Art. 52 penalises payment-institution data violations under the PIPL, Cybersecurity Law and Data Security Law.
Data Security Law adoption and effective dates (commonly 10 Jun 2021 and 1 Sep 2021) were not sourced.

On 17 Aug 2026 the PBOC added eight banks as e-CNY operators (Ping An, Hengfeng, China Bohai, Bank of Shanghai, Bank of Hangzhou, Huishang, Bank of Changsha, Guangxi Beibu Gulf), bringing the total to 30; they start after preparation, no launch date given.

e-CNY research began in 2014, pilots started late 2019, Industrial Bank became the 10th operator in 2022; in October 2025 the PBOC said it would support more banks becoming operators after a pause of over two years; in April 2026 it added 12 banks, with city commercial banks joining for the first time.

The total went from 22 to 30 in the second 2026 expansion; the April batch included Bank of Ningbo, Jiangsu, Beijing, Nanjing and Suzhou (7 not named); the August batch was 3 joint-stock and 5 city commercial banks (secondary).

In the two-tier system the central bank sets business rules and technical standards and builds and runs core infrastructure; commercial banks open wallets, safeguard balances, provide payment services and bear compliance and AML/CTF duties.

The e-CNY technical model is account system + coin strings (币串) + smart contracts, account-based, using blockchain where trust-building is needed; Lu Lei mentions individual, unit and umbrella (伞列) wallets.

The plan upgrades the smart contract service platform, builds an open-source ecosystem and lists applications incl. supply chain finance, carbon inclusion, prepaid fund protection, elder care, utilities, social security, corporate treasury, green energy trading and treasury funds; it calls for building the acceptance environment comprehensively.
To end-November 2025: 3.48 billion (34.8亿笔) cumulative transactions worth RMB 16.7 trillion, 230 million personal wallets via the e-CNY app and 18.84 million unit wallets.
To end-December 2025 CICC cites 3.57 billion transactions worth about RMB 19.5 trillion (secondary).

Wallet tiers (secondary): anonymous tier with mobile number only, RMB 2,000 per payment, RMB 5,000 per day, RMB 10,000 balance; ID-verified bank-linked tier RMB 50,000 per payment, RMB 100,000 per day, RMB 500,000 balance; other categories personal vs corporate, soft vs hard, master wallets with sub-wallets.
CICC says tiers 1 to 3 are real-name wallets earning interest at the demand deposit posted rate and tier 4 is anonymous (phone only), lower limits, no interest (secondary).
Controllable anonymity (可控匿名) is the PBOC's stated privacy principle per secondary sources; Lu Lei's 2025 article does not address privacy.
In July 2023 Bank of China, China Telecom and China Unicom launched SIM-based hard wallets enabling offline NFC payments (secondary).
The PBOC e-CNY White Paper (July 2021) definitions (M0 positioning in 1.0, legal tender, 100% reserve, wallet tiers, controllable anonymity) are cited only via secondary sources.
The PBOC issued the Action Plan; the new-generation measurement framework, management system, operating mechanism and ecosystem formally start on 1 Jan 2026.
Deputy Governor Lu Lei's signed article 守正创新 稳步发展数字人民币 (first in 金融时报) is the primary PBOC voice on the plan.
A customer's e-CNY in a commercial bank wallet is an account-based commercial bank liability, moving from cash-type 1.0 to deposit-money-type 2.0; under 1.0 the liability holder was the central bank.
Banking institutions pay interest on customers' real-name e-CNY wallet balances following the deposit-rate pricing self-discipline agreement; The Paper reports demand-deposit rates.
Bank-wallet e-CNY balances get the same protection as deposits from deposit insurance according to law; the statutory limit is RMB 500,000 per depositor per insured institution.
Bank-type operators' wallet balances are uniformly counted in the reserve-requirement base.

Non-bank payment institutions in e-CNY operations hold a 100% e-CNY margin treated no differently from customer reserve funds; customers convert bank deposits into e-CNY held at the non-bank institution, making it that institution's liability.
e-CNY wallet balances are counted into the corresponding monetary aggregate according to liquidity; no specific aggregate is named.

English government report: the plan classifies digital yuan in commercial bank wallets as bank deposit liabilities; banks will be required to pay interest under deposit rate regulations; balances count toward the reserve base; non-banks must deposit 100 percent reserves against the digital yuan they manage.
Banks can manage wallet balances within asset-liability operations; CICC (secondary) goes further, citing lending or buying wealth management products.
CICC claims 1.0 was M0 and 2.0 enters M1, which PBOC-voice sources do not state (they say only by liquidity).
The Financial News piece says currently at the demand deposit rate and frames the change as moving the liability from central bank to commercial bank; People's Daily reports the same scope.
No full text of the Action Plan was found published; no PBOC statement on M0 treatment of any e-CNY after 1 Jan 2026, or on anonymous wallets, hard wallets or non-bank wallet interest.

Pan Gongsheng announced the international center at the June 2025 Lujiazui Forum as one of eight opening-up measures; official operation was reported 26 Sep 2025 with three platforms (cross-border digital payment, blockchain service, digital asset); platforms 2 and 3 share one blockchain base enabling unified-ledger DvP; principles no harm, compliance and interoperability.
The center is built on the 成方链 base with a unified ledger, separated business domains structure and runs 24/7.

CBETS is a cross-border and blockchain infrastructure service platform for e-CNY built and operated by e-CNY Center International under DCI guidance; on 16 June 2026 26 institutions signed as direct participants incl. Standard Chartered China and branches of Chinese banks in Thailand, Singapore, Laos and Qatar.

CBETS links participants with payment systems of monetary authorities and FIs at home and abroad, supports integration with central bank payment systems and digital currency networks, and offers round-the-clock payment on-chain and off-chain.

Overseas institutions connect through a Hong Kong access point via a unified e-CNY cross-border gateway; named banks ICBC, ABC, BOC, CCB, BoCom, Industrial Bank, CITIC and SPDB; in April 2026 China Southern Power Grid collected Lao electricity payments in e-CNY, cutting settlement from 3 working days to under 5 hours.

CBETS services: 7x24 RMB cross-border digital payments, barcode and tap consumption, remittance, trade and investment settlement; first batch covers Hong Kong, Macau, Singapore, Laos, Thailand, UAE, Qatar and Brazil (secondary citing CCTV).
CBETS is modelled as production with a limited initial participant set since Xinhua describes commercial use; ledger mechanics are not published.

mBridge BIS status is Concluded; founding members HKMA, Bank of Thailand, PBOC DCI and CBUAE (2021); Saudi Central Bank joined 2024; real-value pilot 2022; MVP mid-2024; BIS announced in October 2024 it was handing the project to partners; uses the EVM-compatible mBridge Ledger.
To end-Nov 2025 mBridge carried 4,047 cross-border payments worth about RMB 387.2 billion equivalent, with e-CNY about 95.3% of value; the Action Plan calls for expanding access and lowering costs.

From 17 May 2024 Hong Kong residents can open e-CNY personal wallets with only a Hong Kong mobile number for cross-boundary payments (not P2P) and top up via FPS at 17 retail banks without a mainland account; HKMA calls it the first linkage of a faster payment system with a CBDC system; use extended beyond the GBA; one of six PBOC measures.
CIPS Business Rules took effect 1 Feb 2026, repealing the 2018 rules (Yinfa No. 72 [2018]); the operator is PBOC-approved and the PBOC supervises it and interprets the rules (Arts. 1, 3, 29).

Art. 5: direct participants hold a CIPS account and code; indirect participants have a code but no account and go through a direct participant; Art. 8: zero-balance accounts, one per direct participant, no interest, no overdraft, zero at day end.

Art. 9: the operator may hold settlement funds in a segregated clearing account at the PBOC, not commercial bank accounts; Art. 17: hybrid RTGS for single payments and designated-time net settlement for batch, plus PvP, DvP and CCP clearing; Art. 18: insufficient-balance payments queued in expedited and regular queues.
Art. 19: RTGS payments are irrevocable once sender debited and receiver credited, net-settled payments once netting completes; Art. 28: operator sets message standards.

CIPS hours are 5x24 hours + 4 hours: day session 8:30 to 17:30 Beijing time (cut-off 17:00), night session 17:00 to 08:30 (cut-off 08:00); on the first day after a holiday the day session starts 04:30.

HVPS funding (hvps.112) must be done by 09:00, with night pre-funding via hvps.115 from 16:00 to 17:00; zeroing returns balances to the originating HVPS clearing account; message identifiers include cips.111 (customer payment), cips.113 (batch) and cips.303 (cancel); netting results and CCP settlement cannot be cancelled.
CIPS message standards are formulated on ISO 20022 methodology; current versions V3.0.1 and HKD V1.0.1 (23 Mar 2026).

CIPS offers discrete RTGS and batch netting modes, direct links to CCDC, Shanghai Clearing House, HK CMU and CFETS, cross-border RMB e-wallet settlement under the clearing-institution lending business, and HKD business since Sep 2021 (09:00 to 17:00).
CIPS volume: August 2026 791,000 payments worth RMB 19.4 trillion; January to August 2026 6.023 million payments worth RMB 139.7 trillion.
As of September 2026 CIPS had 214 direct and 1,651 indirect participants; operator address 100 Zhongshan South Road, Huangpu, Shanghai.

As of end-June 2026 CIPS had 210 direct and 1,619 indirect participants in 130 countries and regions reaching 5,200+ legal-entity banks in 192 countries and regions; volumes RMB 180.2 trillion in 2025 (+2.7%) and RMB 100.9 trillion in H1 2026 (+11.9%) (secondary citing PBOC report released 24 Sep 2026).

CIPS phase 1 started 8 Oct 2015 with 19 direct participants and phase 2 fully started 2 May 2018; the PBOC is the largest shareholder (16%) with foreign shareholders incl. HSBC and Standard Chartered; SWIFT MoU March 2016 and SWIFT messaging carries over 80% of CIPS transactions (secondary).
The CIPS English home page shows an Asia sub-count (148 direct / 1,157 indirect) inconsistent with its regional breakdown (Asia 1,176 indirect).

In the domestic QR scenario, a same-bank transfer is plausibly an on-us book entry; a cross-operator transfer must cross PBOC central e-CNY infrastructure, with the settlement asset for that leg not publicly specified.

Only cash, central bank reserves and CBDC are claims on (or property backed by) the central bank; commercial bank money is issued under prudential regulation (atlas money taxonomy takeaway, framed on BIS AER 2025).

Cash: ledger of record is the physical object; typical rail is hand to hand; protection on issuer failure: central bank does not fail in the ordinary sense (inference); regime: central bank law and legal tender statutes (not sourced here).
BIS frames central bank reserves as 'the highest form of money' and the ultimate settlement asset.
BIS 'three tests' of money are singleness (settle at par, enabled by final settlement in central bank reserves), elasticity and integrity.
Central bank money is the 'trust anchor' for singleness.
Pontes: final settlement of the cash leg occurs once completed in T2.
Tokenisation 'does not alter the legal characterisation' of central bank reserves and commercial bank deposits or their obligations.
Retail CBDC is generally a central bank liability: a claim in some jurisdictions, property in others.

In two-tier models the legal framework should keep retail CBDC a direct central bank liability unaffected by intermediary insolvency; if holdings at intermediaries are classed as ordinary deposits users could face delays or losses, so at least proprietary rights should attach (IMF pp. 4, 19 to 20).
Platform 'accounts' can be mere identification tools or financial accounts; if financial, they may be current accounts (repayment on demand) or safeguarding accounts (fiduciary duties) (IMF p. 19).
CBDC is defined in the US executive order as digital money in the national unit of account that is a direct liability of the central bank.
Offline and online CBDC should both be legal tender and convertible at par (IMF pp. 29 to 30).
BIS CBDC dataset (WP 880), last updated March 2024, reported four live retail CBDCs and retail pilots in 24 jurisdictions at that time.

BIS 2024 survey (Paper 159, 22 Aug 2025): 93 central banks responded; 91% (85) exploring retail, wholesale or both; wholesale work more advanced in aggregate; more than one in three accelerated work in response to stablecoins and crypto.

Wholesale CBDC is a tokenised form of reserves for a predefined group; tokens typically reflect rights against the central bank, often linked to RTGS accounts; the link to reserves should ideally be enshrined in law (IMF p. 31).
Desynchronisation between token ledgers and RTGS is a key legal risk (double spending or unbacked tokens) (IMF p. 31).
Commercial bank money is issued under prudential regulation and deposit guarantees.
Tokenised commercial bank money settles in central bank reserves at par and the payee simply holds a larger claim on her own bank.
FDIC insures deposits 'to at least $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category at each FDIC-insured bank'.

FSCS deposit protection limit rose to GBP 120,000 per eligible person per bank on 1 Dec 2025 (firms failing after 30 Nov 2025); qualifying temporary high balances are protected up to GBP 1.4 million for six months.
EU e-money is monetary value stored electronically representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds and accepted by third parties (EMD2 Art 2(2)).
Funds received by an e-money issuer 'shall not constitute either a deposit' (EMD2 Art 6(3)).
E-money funds are safeguarded under PSD rules (EMD2 Art 7); redemption is at par at any time (Art 11); no interest or time-related benefit may be granted (Art 12).
Non-bank e-money is a complement to bank money, usually held with commercial banks.

UK safeguarding is mandatory for authorised payment institutions, authorised e-money institutions and small e-money institutions (a condition of authorisation or registration), optional for small payment institutions; methods are segregation or insurance or comparable guarantee.
UK safeguarding is 'a condition of authorisation' for APIs, AEMIs and SEMIs; methods are segregation or insurance/comparable guarantee.

FCA safeguarding page updated 7 May 2026 'following new safeguarding rules coming into effect', with a supplementary regime in CASS 15 and CASS 10A (daily reconciliations, resolution packs, audits, monthly REP027 return).
Tokenised deposits give a direct claim on the issuing bank and are redeemable at par for central bank money.
Tokenisation 'does not alter the legal characterisation' of commercial bank deposits.

JPMorgan describes a tokenised deposit as 'a digital representation of a commercial bank deposit recorded on a blockchain network'; JPM Coin is 'not a cryptocurrency or a stablecoin', is backed by USD deposits at J.P. Morgan and redeemable to USD on the client's account at any time.
Deposit-insurance coverage (for example FDIC or FSCS) of a specific deposit token was not explicitly confirmed by any source opened; expected by legal analysis.
Stablecoins are digital bearer instruments; stablecoin holders have bilateral claims on each issuer and prices can deviate from par.
BIS finds stablecoins perform poorly on singleness, elasticity and integrity and 'cannot be the mainstay of the future monetary system'.

Stablecoin market capitalisation was about USD 320 billion at end-May 2026; about 99.4% of fiat-backed stablecoins by value are USD-pegged; estimated 2025 volume about USD 28 trillion gross but about USD 390 billion a year adjusted (Visa-based).

MiCA: e-money tokens reference one official currency and are deemed electronic money; issuer must be a credit institution or e-money institution; holders have a claim on the issuer and redemption at par at any time; no interest (recitals 18, 19, 66 to 68, 70; article text not rendered in fetch).
MiCA recital 13: central bank money in digital form issued by central banks acting as monetary authority is outside MiCA.

US GENIUS Act signed 18 Jul 2025: 100% reserves in liquid assets such as USD and short-term Treasuries, monthly public reserve disclosure, holders have priority over all other creditors on issuer insolvency, issuers barred from misleadingly claiming federal insurance, government backing or legal tender status.
Unbacked cryptoassets are speculative assets rather than money (BIS).
FDIC deposit insurance does not cover crypto assets.
From 1 Jan 2026, e-CNY in commercial-bank wallets is classified as bank deposit liabilities, earns interest under deposit-rate rules and is covered by deposit insurance.
Under the 2026 framework non-bank payment institutions must hold 100% reserves against e-CNY they manage.
Cumulative e-CNY usage to end-Nov 2025: 3.48 billion transactions worth CNY 16.7 trillion.

Eight operators were added on 17 Aug 2026 (Ping An, Hengfeng, China Bohai, Bank of Shanghai, Bank of Hangzhou, Huishang, Bank of Changsha, Guangxi Beibu Gulf), taking the total from 22 to 30; 12 had been added in Apr 2026; new operators start only after preparations complete.
Timeline: research from 2014; trials began late 2019; in Oct 2025 the PBOC said it would support more operators; the Xinhua article does not use 'nationwide' or 'pilot' for the current state.

India amended the RBI Act to cover digital banknotes.

The UK has neither decided to issue nor abandoned the digital pound.
Digital pound would be non-interest-bearing.

A prototype ledger experiment is under way and a deferred offline design note has been published.
The BoE plans to test synchronisation of RTGS with tokenised transactions in 2026 before production deployment, alongside wCBDC experimentation and the RT2 upgrade.

Agorá scope: multi-currency shared programmable platform for wholesale cross-border payments using tokenised central bank reserves and tokenised commercial bank deposits for atomic settlement.

Next phase: Agorá intends real-value transactions with certain currencies and participants, with an 'enhanced role for the private sector' and continued central bank engagement.

Dunbar built two multi-CBDC prototypes (Corda by R3, Quorum by Partior); findings published 22 Mar 2022; hybrid access via sponsoring local banks; BIS label 'Concluded'.
Icebreaker tested a hub-and-spoke link between experimental retail CBDC systems, splitting payments into two domestic legs with competing FX providers; report 6 Mar 2023; BIS label 'Concluded'.
Post-quantum cryptography will be needed for CBDC, but Project Tourbillon found much slower performance.

JPM Coin benefits from existing regulatory deposit frameworks.

BIS defines three retail architectures: direct (one-tier, fully operated by the central bank), hybrid (PSPs onboard and process; central bank also records retail balances and can act as backstop if a PSP fails) and intermediated (central bank records only wholesale balances of each PSP).
Most central bank laws do not let the central bank open current accounts for the public, so most designs are two-tier.

BIS 2021: account-based CBDC requires user identification (digital ID); token-based uses password-like digital signatures without identification; a token-based CBDC with full anonymity could facilitate illegal activity; most promising is account-based built on digital ID.
NY Fed economists argue account-based and token-based are not mutually exclusive (Bitcoin satisfies both) and suggest revising or retiring the terms.

IMF reframes account versus token legally: whether holdings carry proprietary title ring-fenced from intermediaries, and whether platform accounts are identifiers, current accounts or safeguarding accounts.

BIS system design: data models range from centralised to decentralised hub-and-spoke to peer-to-peer; a modular hybrid with centralised core settlement and decentralised identity/key management is suggested; peer-to-peer may not suit core settlement.
A BIS unified ledger 'may or may not use distributed ledger technology'.

Offline CBDC is exchanged without network connection or third-party arbiter; immediate mode settles device to device, deferred mode settles on reconnection; mitigations include holding limits, limits on forward transactions, limits on time offline, secure hardware and certification; interest on offline balances may be hard to implement.
Settlement solely in the central bank's system may eliminate or minimise double-spend risk.
Law must define when offline settlement is final; roles and liability for double spending must be defined; device loss may mean loss of funds.

Privacy by design plus privacy by policy, compatible with AML/CFT; PETs (homomorphic encryption, MPC, ZKPs, confidential computing) add latency and complexity; tiered user-chosen privacy adds complexity and consent disputes.
BIS 2021: separate payment services from control over payment data; law enforcement access only in exceptional cases.

Holding caps must be 'clearly grounded in law', set primarily by the central bank; waterfalls into bank accounts raise property-rights issues and require transparency, proportionality and user consent.
Transaction limits need a legal basis (Russia's law empowers the Bank of Russia to set maximum digital ruble transaction amounts).
Fee caps need cost-linked justification and proportionality, else they may be seen as reducing face value.

Most retail CBDC projects are unremunerated; Russia bans interest; BoE digital pound zero interest; Bank of Israel considering interest-bearing CBDC; an interest-bearing CBDC's market value may diverge from nominal value (par convertibility concern).

Programmable money (currency encoded with use restrictions such as expiry or goods limits) is largely rejected for property-rights, expropriation and discrimination concerns and needs explicit legal authorisation; programmable payments (user-initiated, condition-triggered) do not change the currency; liability for code errors must be allocated.
BIS multi-CBDC models: enhanced compatibility, interlinking, and a single multi-CBDC system (PvP by default).
Compatibility with existing EMV terminals matters; a BoE proof of concept indicated existing terminals could in principle initiate CBDC payments without modification.
Under attributed powers 'a central bank must have statutory authority to issue rCBDC'; most central bank laws do not clearly allow it; explicit legislation recommended.
Some jurisdictions compel distribution: Nigeria requires all licensed FIs to act as eNaira intermediaries; mandates must be proportionate.

'CBDC is a government stablecoin' is wrong: CBDC is a direct central bank liability, stablecoins are private liabilities with reserve requirements and insolvency priority, and MiCA excludes central bank digital money.
BIS distinguishes tokenised deposits (claim on issuing bank, par redeemable for central bank money) from stablecoins (bearer instruments).
Stablecoins and crypto are not deposit-insured: FDIC does not cover crypto assets and GENIUS bars misleading federal-insurance claims.

ISO 20022-1:2026 'Part 1: Metamodel', Edition 3, 154 pages, published (stage 60.60) on 2026-04-13 by ISO/TC 68/SC 9, replaces the withdrawn ISO 20022-1:2013; it defines the metamodel used to create and maintain message standards, not individual messages.
ISO 20022-2:2013 (UML profile), Edition 3, published 2013-05-07, was last reviewed and confirmed in 2024 and 'remains current'; it replaced ISO 20022-2:2007.

iso20022.org says the current edition 'includes nine parts, published in April 2026' and describes ISO 20022 as a single standardisation approach (methodology, process, repository) with a central dictionary and XML and ASN.1 design rules.

The catalogue lists 807 messages grouped into business domains (Payments, Securities, Trade Finance, Cards, FX) and business areas with four-letter codes (pacs, pain, camt, acmt, reda, colr, fxtr, caaa, casp, catp); identifiers follow a dotted pattern such as pacs.008.001.14.

For each message set iso20022.org provides Message Definition Reports, Message Usage Guidelines where needed, XSD schemas and Business Application Header documentation; it recommends the most recent version and archives older ones.

Development and maintenance are driven by catalogued business justifications (messages, API resources, supplementary data, variants) and change requests (message definitions, API resources, external code sets, data source schemes, supplementary data, business model).

Governance: ISO TC 68/SC 9 oversees; the Registration Management Group oversees registration and defines business domains; Standards Evaluation Groups (Payments, Securities, Cards and Related Retail Financial Services, FX, Trade Finance, API Resources) validate new definitions and approve changes; a Technical Support Group and a Cross SEG Harmonisation Group support; procedures approved October 2021.

The Registration Authority is operated by SWIFT S.C.; it oversees the Financial Repository and iso20022.org, checks repository items against approved technical specifications and publishes the repository on ISO's behalf.

GLEIF is a Swiss foundation established in 2014, backed by the G20 and FSB, overseen by the Regulatory Oversight Committee created by the 2012 LEI Charter.

PCI PIN Security covers secure management, processing and transmission of PINs and keys, is intended for acquirers and agents processing PIN transactions, and whether an entity must comply or validate is decided by compliance-programme owners such as a payment brand or acquirer.
PCI P2PE covers solutions, components and applications that encrypt account data from capture in the merchant device to decryption at the provider.
PCI MPoC is a modular, objective-based standard for accepting both PIN and contactless card data on the same COTS device, building on SPoC and CPoC; an errata bulletin for v1.0.1 is linked.
PCI 3DS SDK, CPoC and SPoC are in a formal sunset period from 1 May to 31 October 2026; PA-DSS retired 28 October 2022, superseded by Secure Software and Secure SLC.

GENIUS Act signed 18 July 2025 (passed Congress 17 July 2025); effective on the earlier of 18 January 2027 or 120 days after the primary federal payment stablecoin regulators issue final implementing regulations.
As of early October 2026 none of the primary-regulator GENIUS rules (OCC, FDIC, NCUA, Fed) is final; only Treasury's state-certification procedures are an interim final rule.
Arnold & Porter (8 Oct 2026) says no rule is final and final rules are expected 'in the coming weeks', with full-implementation timing uncertain.
Secondary press reports the Fed missed the statutory one-year rulemaking deadline (18 July 2026), pushing effectiveness toward 18 January 2027 (low reliability).

PPSI paths reflected in agency rulemakings: subsidiary of an insured depository institution approved by its federal regulator (FDIC for FDIC-supervised banks, Fed for insured state member banks, OCC for national banks, NCUA for credit unions); federal qualified nonbank issuer chartered and supervised by the OCC; state qualified issuer under a Treasury-certified 'substantially similar' state regime, available only at or below USD 10 billion consolidated outstanding issuance.
Above USD 10 billion a state-qualified uninsured PPSI must transition to the federal framework within 360 days or stop new issuance unless the Board grants a waiver (Fed proposal).

Fed proposal: identifiable, segregated reserves with fair value at least equal to outstanding par at all times (1:1); eligible assets limited to US coin and currency, Federal Reserve Bank balances, eligible deposit claims, Treasuries with 93 days or less remaining maturity, Treasury-backed overnight repo and reverse repo, qualifying government MMFs holding only such assets, Board-approved federal assets and certain tokenised forms.

OCC proposed a 40% single-institution limit on deposits plus further concentration, weighted-average-maturity and minimum insured-deposit holdings for large PPSIs; FDIC proposed only a 40% single eligible institution limit.

Fed proposal on redemption: public redemption policy; redemption generally within two business days of a request; extensions only at Board discretion for safety and soundness, financial stability or public interest; fee changes need seven days' notice; minimum redemption one payment stablecoin.

Fed proposal on attestation: monthly reserve composition reports certified by CEO and CFO and examined by a registered public accounting firm (an examination, distinct from a full financial statement audit).

Fed proposal on capital: 2% credit-risk charge on reserves held as uninsured deposit claims or undercollateralised reverse repo; operational-risk charge of 2.0% on the first USD 20bn outstanding, 1.5% on the next USD 30bn and 1.0% above USD 50bn, plus 25% of three-year average non-reserve revenue; USD 5m de novo floor.

Reserve shortfall: Fed proposal requires a remediation plan after one quarter-end shortfall and liquidation and redemption after a second consecutive quarter; OCC proposal requires liquidation after 15 consecutive business days of reserve shortfall.
The Fed framework proposal applies the tying prohibition to all PPSIs and covers custodians of payment stablecoins and reserves.
Until final rules issue no entity holds a GENIUS PPSI approval; existing USD stablecoins operate under pre-GENIUS state money-transmitter and trust frameworks (inference).

On 17 September 2026 the SEC granted five-year exemptive relief for tokenised NMS stock (Rel. No. 34-106402) for certain permissioned venues and liquidity providers.

Because USDC is multi-issued (EU and US entities issue fungible tokens), the significance decision and the multi-issuance debate are intertwined (inference).

Per ESMA, non-EU firms may not serve or solicit EU clients except by reverse solicitation (including B2B); MiCA protections attach only to the authorised entity, not group affiliates sharing a brand.

HMT Payments Forward Plan timeline: FCA issuance rules policy statement Q2 to Q3 2026, BoE systemic stablecoin final rules by end-2026, FCA crypto regime live October 2027.

MAS MD Chia Der Jiun (9 October 2026 keynote): deposit tokens hold par via exchangeability for central bank reserves, while stablecoins lack that anchor.

Ethereum PoS uses 12-second slots and 32-slot epochs; checkpoint pairs attracting two-thirds of staked ETH become justified and then finalised; reverting a finalised block would cost an attacker at least one-third of total staked ETH (2 epochs x 32 slots x 12 s = 768 s is arithmetic, not a stated figure).
