The issuer is the bank that services cardholder accounts; it authorises, clears and settles transactions and is ultimately responsible to the network for its agents.
The acquirer serves merchants, typically by direct contract, submits merchant clearing data and receives settlement credits for the merchants it sponsors.
The network collects transactions, operates the gateway, sets rules and formats and facilitates settlement among client banks; it does not issue cards or contract directly with merchants.
Processors and other third parties do processing, IT and specialty work in the card supply chain.

A four-party scheme runs payments from payer's to payee's account through the intermediation of the scheme, an issuer and an acquirer; in a three-party scheme the scheme itself provides acquiring and issuing (Art 2(17)-(18)).
A three-party scheme that licenses other PSPs to issue or acquire, or issues with a co-branding partner or through an agent, is treated as a four-party scheme (Art 1(5)).
Card schemes and processing entities must be independent in accounting, organisation and decision-making; bundled pricing and cross-subsidy between scheme and processing are banned (Art 7).

Stripe Issuing describes card programmes built on partner banks plus Visa and Mastercard; the platform can approve or decline in real time, set spending controls and must fund an Issuing balance before spend (vendor).
Stripe states Issuing is available in the US, UK and many EEA countries and stablecoin-backed card programmes in more than 30 countries (vendor; pointer only).
A Visa Direct Originator must be a licensed Visa acquirer or a third-party originator sponsored by one.
Visa Token Service is aimed at issuers, merchants, developers and small-business issuers across all Visa regions (vendor).
Authorisation occurs at purchase, checks card validity, account status and available funds, and creates records at merchant and issuer, including for declines.

ISO 8583 MTI digits: version (0=1987, 1=1993, 2=2003), class (1 authorisation, 2 financial, 4 reversal/chargeback, 5 reconciliation, 8 network management), function, origin; 0100/0110 authorisation, 0200/0210 financial, 0220 financial advice, 0400/0420 reversal, 0800 network management; proprietary variants exist (secondary).

Dual-message (credit and signature debit): merchants batch drafts at least daily, the network sorts them to issuers, issuers match and drop against authorisations; single-message (PIN, Maestro, foreign ATM) authorises and clears in one step with one daily cutoff; US PIN is single-message and Europe used dual-message for all (as of 2013).
Mastercard clearing systems named in the 2013 tutorial: GCMS for dual-message and MDS for single-message.

EMV 3DS helps issuers and merchants prevent CNP fraud: merchant sends transaction, payment method and device data; low-risk transactions approved without extra steps, higher-risk ones may need OTP, knowledge-based questions or biometrics.
EMVCo lists a draft v2.4.0.0 (comment period ended 1 July 2026), a bulletin covering v2.2.0 to 2.3.1.1, and recommends v2.2 or higher.

EMVCo defines Token Requestors (registered with a TSP, Token Requestor ID), TSPs issuing tokens on behalf of issuers, usage types (device-specific, merchant-specific, guest checkout, token user), the token cryptogram as a token control field, domain restriction controls, ID&V-based token assurance and lifecycle events.

An authorisation holds the amount; uncaptured authorisations expire; validity windows: CNP Visa 5 days merchant-initiated (exactly 4 days 18 hours) and 7 days customer-initiated; Mastercard, Amex, Discover 7 days; card-present Visa 5 days, others 2 days (vendor).
Partial capture releases the remainder; most payments allow one capture; issuer statements may not distinguish authorisations from captures (vendor).
The 18 April 2026 Visa Core Rules contain Section 7.3.7 Authorization Reversals and Authorization Holds and Table 5-14 Authorization Reversal Requirement (text not extracted).

Clearing is a non-monetary exchange of transaction data usually completed within one day for dual-message; settlement is the monetary exchange usually within about two days for dual-message; single-message settlement is tied to the daily cutoff.

Net settlement uses one window for both message types with aggregate net positions per client bank; net debtors remit to the network clearing account and net creditors are paid; all funds flow through the network's settlement account at a chosen settlement bank.
All net settlement funds flow through the network's settlement account at a chosen settlement bank.
Issuers are mostly net debtors (purchases) with credits from returns and cash disbursements; acquirers are mostly net creditors with debits from refunds, returns and chargebacks.

In the US many issuers pre-authorise Fedwire drawdowns (1031 request answered by 1032 transfer), more common for USD dual-message GCMS connections; single-message MDS connections more likely settle by ACH; most credits and debits move within about an hour after cutoff, Monday to Friday.
VisaNet is the global network for Visa credit, debit and ATM transactions, used to authorise transactions, with a six nines (99.9999%) availability standard.
Acquirers credit merchants according to contract; most merchants are credited within 24 hours of drafts entering settlement; some keep funds at the acquirer, others at a separate depository bank.

For sales interchange is paid by the acquirer to the issuer; for cash advances, withdrawals, credits and returns the issuer pays the acquirer; rates set by the network; assessed during clearing and added to or deducted from net settlement.
Consumer debit interchange is capped at 0.2% and consumer credit at 0.3% per transaction; Member States may set lower domestic caps; MDR is the fee the payee pays the acquirer.

Covered issuers' debit interchange must be reasonable and proportional to cost (small issuers, government programmes and certain reloadable prepaid exempt); a fraud-prevention adjustment is available; at least two unaffiliated networks; no inhibiting merchant routing.
Final rule 29 June 2011, updated 3 October 2022; on 25 October 2023 the Board proposed lowering the cap; status not stated on the page last updated 17 May 2024.
Declines are recorded at merchant and issuer like approvals.
Effective 25 July 2026 Visa added Visa-only response code RC 83 Fraud/Security for transactions declined by STIP due to high-risk or fraudulent conditions (Section 7.3.6.3).

Visa dispute categories: 10 Fraud, 11 Authorisation, 12 Processing Errors, 13 Consumer Disputes; Section 11 has per-condition Dispute Time Limit tables and pre-arbitration requirements; 11.11 arbitration; 11.12 compliance.

Visa dispute lifecycle runs cardholder to issuer, issuer to acquirer, acquirer to merchant; merchant accepts or rejects with documentation via the acquirer; each step has a time limit that may vary by acquirer.

Condition 12.2 covers a credit processed where a reversal was needed or vice versa; Condition 12.6: if the customer paid by another method the merchant should reverse; duplicates should be reversed; credits processed promptly.
Visa stage names Dispute Response, Pre-Arbitration, Pre-Arbitration Response and Arbitration appear in Visa Business News (23 April 2020).

Under Visa Claims Resolution, Allocation covers fraud and authorisation (10.x, 11.x) with rules-based liability; Collaboration covers processing errors and consumer disputes (12.x, 13.x); there is no universal 30-day merchant response window; an acquirer example gives 9 or 18 calendar days (secondary).

For dual-message each reason code follows Issuer Chargeback, Acquirer Second Presentment, Issuer Pre-arbitration Case, Acquirer Response, Issuer Arbitration Case, Acquirer Response; single-message uses chargeback, representment and in some cases automated reversal.

Mastercard time frames (secondary, uncited): first chargeback up to 120 days after transaction in most cases; second presentment 45 days; 30 days to open pre-arbitration and 30 to respond; 15 days to escalate to arbitration.
If a chargeback is resolved for the cardholder, the network debits the acquirer's net settlement and credits the issuer's.
ISO 8583 class 4 covers reversals and chargebacks (0400/0420) (secondary).
Issuers match clearing drafts to prior authorisations (match and drop).

The correspondent holds deposits owned by respondent banks and provides payment and other services; banks settle by crediting and debiting those accounts; CPMI uses 'loro account' for the account bank B holds for bank A.

Serial (MT 103) and cover (MT 202 COV) methods can both be AML/CFT compliant if all fields are accurately populated; banks choose and agree with counterparties; nested respondents reach the correspondent through a direct respondent.

CPMI recommended KYC utilities, LEI use in correspondent banking (BIC-to-LEI mapping), information sharing (KYCC clarification), payment message content guidance and optional LEI in MT 103/202 COV and future ISO 20022.

De-risking drivers: insufficient volume to cover compliance cost, risky jurisdictions, insufficient customer information, high-risk products/customers, rising compliance cost and KYCC uncertainty, post-crisis deleveraging.

Active correspondent relationships fell about 20% over seven years and corridors about 10% (May 2019); Americas excluding North America lost about 30% since 2012; 15 jurisdictions had fewer than 20 relationships in 2018.
Relationships declined 4% in 2020 and about 25% between 2011 and 2020 while cross-border payment volume rose 2% and value 7% in 2020 (SWIFT data, over 200 jurisdictions).
The number of active correspondent banks fell 22% from 2011 (September 2020 report, secondary).
The UETR is a 36-character reference generated by the ordering institution in field 121; intermediaries must not create a new one and must pass it on; cover payments copy the original UETR.
From end 2020 all member banks must confirm payment status to the Tracker when funds are credited, including rejections.
gpi features (2018): same-day use of funds, total fee and time transparency, end-to-end tracking, unaltered field 70 remittance information, ACSC status confirmation, UETR, gpi Stop and Recall.
Swift states nearly 60% of gpi payments are credited to end beneficiaries within 30 minutes and almost 100% within 24 hours (undated statistic), over USD 300 billion daily.

End of coexistence for cross-border payment instructions was 22 November 2025; afterwards no FIN MT payment instructions are delivered and contingency processing is active; opt out of in-flow translation by 19 December 2025 to avoid charges.
ISO 20022 instructions averaged over 60% of Swift daily cross-border volume in September 2025.

Hybrid addresses available after 22 November 2025; fully unstructured addresses removed November 2026 with payments lacking structured town and country rejected; case management (camt.110/111, camt.056/029) mandatory November 2027; automated Tracker confirmations for received pacs.008 required.

Contingency processing and in-flow translation are chargeable from 1 January 2026 outside Fixed fee and Swift Essentials; MT sent after coexistence are validated and converted; MT 199/299 remain supported with no end date but deprecated.

Mapping (industry practice): MT103 to pacs.008; MT202 to pacs.009; MT202COV to pacs.009 COV; returns to pacs.004; MT192/292 to camt.056; MT196/296 to camt.029; MT900/910 to camt.054; MT940/950 to camt.053.
Converting ISO 20022 to MT mid-chain can lose data; messages failing validation are NACKed; MT103/202 REJT/RETN are also affected (vendor).

CLS settles FX trades individually and gross, PvP, through central bank accounts; CLS Bank International (New York) is regulated and overseen by the Federal Reserve as an Edge Act corporation with a CLS Oversight Committee coordinated by the New York Fed; 18 currencies.
CLS currencies: AUD, CAD, DKK, EUR, HKD, HUF, ILS, JPY, KRW, MXN, NZD, NOK, SGD, ZAR, SEK, CHF, GBP, USD.
CLS has over 75 settlement members and over 38,000 third-party users; multilateral netting reduces funding by over 96% on average.

2015 snapshot: 62 settlement members, about 18,000 third parties, accounts at 17 central banks with RTGS access, FX spot, forwards and swaps, settlement final and irrevocable, about USD 5.1 trillion average daily value needing under USD 50 billion funding.

INR is not a CLS currency; CCIL acts as a third-party aggregator via settlement member UBS Switzerland AG; CCIL states a CLS settlement window of 7:00 to 12:00 CET and trade reporting cutoff 8:30 pm IST on S-1.

Card currency conversion charges must be expressed as a percentage mark-up over the latest ECB euro reference rates and disclosed before payment; for online credit transfers with conversion the PSP shows estimated conversion charges, total debit and estimated amount received.
Wise says it uses the mid-market rate with no exchange-rate markup and shows fees before confirmation (vendor).
Wise says it built its own network using local bank accounts to avoid SWIFT; senders pay in domestically and Wise pays out from its account in the destination country (vendor).
Wise Q2 2026 (April to June 2026): 77% of transfers instant (under 20 seconds), 97% within a day; connected to UPI in India and other local systems (vendor).

OCT pushes funds to the account linked to a recipient's Visa card; AFT pulls funds like a purchase; domestic and cross-border; the originator is responsible for end-to-end settlement, disputes and reporting; funds availability varies by receiving institution, account type, region and corridor.
Visa Direct supports P2P, disbursements, bill pay and cross-border remittances; recipients need an eligible debit or prepaid card.
Mastercard Move: 200+ countries and territories, 150+ currencies, 95% of banked population, about 17 billion endpoints across accounts, cards, wallets and cash pickup (vendor, as of October 2025).

UPI-PayNow launched 21 February 2023; users send via UPI ID, mobile number or VPA; initial limit INR 60,000 per day (about SGD 1,000); operators NIPL and BCS; initial banks SBI, IOB, Indian Bank, ICICI (in and out), Axis and DBS India (inward), DBS Singapore and Liquid Group.

Nexus has been a BIS Innovation Hub project since 2022 with a blueprint in July 2024; in 2025 the central banks of India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand incorporated Nexus Global Payments and the BIS handed over; target payments within 60 seconds in most cases.
NGP was established on 26 March 2025 by central banks and IPS operators of India, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand as a not-for-profit in Singapore; 'Nexus is not yet operational'.
A September 2024 article projected Nexus go-live in 2026 (secondary).
The CPMI final report on governance and oversight of FPS interlinking was published 15 October 2024.

End-2027 targets: retail cost global average at or below 1% with no corridor above 3%; remittances at or below 3% for USD 200 by 2030 with no corridor above 5%; 75% within one hour and the remainder within one business day; over 90% of individuals able to access electronic remittances; minimum transparency set; no wholesale cost target.

2025 KPIs: wholesale more than 50% within one hour and above 90% within one business day; retail P2P cost about 2.5%; retail 35.4% within one hour and 67.3% within one business day; remittance cost 6.5% for USD 200 and 4.3% for USD 500; 54.4% of remittance services within one hour; 78.7% of adults hold a transaction account; 62.9% of cost-transparent providers disclose speed.

The FSB says most Roadmap actions are complete but satisfactory global improvements are unlikely by 2027; FATF revised Recommendation 16; jurisdictions urged to improve domestic systems as first and last mile.
FATF revised Recommendation 16 (mentioned in the FSB press release of 9 October 2025).
Reg E 1005.30 defines remittance transfer and provider, with a safe harbour for 500 or fewer transfers in the previous and current year; transfers of USD 15 or less excluded.
Reg E 1005.31 requires a prepayment disclosure (amount, fees, taxes, total, exchange rate, amount to recipient) and a receipt with date available and rights.
Reg E 1005.34 allows cancellation if requested within 30 minutes of payment and funds not picked up or deposited; refund within three business days.
Regulation (EU) 2021/1230 Art 3 makes euro cross-border charges equal to domestic charges.
UK PSRs 2017 reg 43 requires information before a single payment contract including maximum execution time, charges and actual or reference exchange rate.
LRS allows resident individuals up to USD 250,000 per financial year; PAN mandatory; via Authorised Dealer banks.
NEFT runs 24x7 in half-hourly batches, owned and operated by RBI; returns within two hours of batch end if credit fails; usable for inward foreign remittances.
IMPS is a 24x7 instant interbank transfer service with bank-prescribed limits.
The ledger balance is the account balance not reduced by any holds from pending transactions.
The available balance is generally the ledger balance plus uncleared deposits made available, minus pending (authorised but unsettled) debits; pending debits reduce available but not ledger balance.
APSN example (CFPB Table 1): USD 100 available; USD 50 card purchase day 1; USD 120 ACH debit settles day 2 with USD 34 fee; USD 50 purchase settles day 3 triggering a second fee.

Posted balance is the sum of posted entries; pending balance the sum of pending plus posted; available balance treats pending outflows as gone and pending inflows as not arrived, the safest approach for approving a transaction (vendor).

A ledger transaction is mutable while pending and immutable once posted; corrections add entries (offset and repost, or difference); states pending, posted, archived; the immutable ledger is the source of truth separate from mutable business objects (vendor).
Bank transfers may take up to three days to settle while ledger entries stay pending (vendor).

Idempotency: client generates a unique key per operation (Stripe Idempotency-Key header on POST); server binds key to request state, returns cached result on replay or resumes a failed attempt; covers request never arriving, server failing midway, or lost response; ACID rollback; retries with exponential backoff and jitter.

End customers of a custodial (FBO) account are each insured up to the per-bank limit only if the custodial relationship is disclosed in deposit account records and the FDIC can determine owners and interests from records kept in good faith and the regular course of business (secondary).

The FDIC Recordkeeping for Custodial Accounts NPRM (RIN 3064-AG07) was published 2 Oct 2024 (89 FR 80135); the Unified Agenda lists it as a Long-Term Action with final action To Be Determined; not withdrawn.

The proposal covers custodial deposit accounts with transactional features, with exemptions (trust-only, government, broker-dealer/investment adviser, IOLTA, benefit-plan, certain mortgage-servicing).

Banks would identify each beneficial owner, balance and ownership category in an FDIC electronic format and reconcile at least as of close of each business day; a third-party recordkeeper only with direct, continuous and unrestricted access incl. during insolvency, contractual daily reconciliation, independent validation and bank-held backups; annual CEO/COO certification and report.
Trustee status report (20 Jun 2024): potential shortfall of USD 65m to 96m between FBO balances and amounts owed per Synapse's records.

Evolve held about USD 46.9m in payment-processing accounts for Synapse and reported numerous material discrepancies in Synapse Brokerage ledgers, citing a Yotta ledger showing USD 109m on 11 Apr 2024 and USD 1.4m on 17 May 2024 with no matching transfers.
Lineage held USD 61.8m in a single FBO account for Synapse.
AMG released about USD 99m to over 31,000 end users.

Synapse spread one customer's funds across several banks; large pre-bankruptcy interbank transfers were not allocated to end users or fintechs; the trustee needed admin access to Synapse's MongoDB and AWS systems to rebuild records.

CFPB filed suit and a stipulated judgment on 21 Aug 2025 alleging Synapse failed to track consumers' funds and match partner banks' records; relief: USD 1 civil money penalty, injunctive relief, ban on selling customer data.

CFPB approved USD 46,248,291 from the Civil Penalty Fund on 28 Nov 2025, about half the estimated USD 65m to 95m shortfall; aggregate owed around USD 265m against USD 219m bank holdings; figures inconsistent (USD 60m to 95m also cited).
EMD2 Art 7 requires safeguarding, Art 11 par redemption and Art 12 prohibits interest on e-money.
FCA CASS 15 is in force from 7 May 2026 with internal and external reconciliations, monthly safeguarding return, resolution pack and annual audit.

TPRM guidance finalised 6 Jun 2023, published 9 Jun 2023; life cycle of planning, due diligence, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring, termination plus governance; rescinds FRB SR 13-19, FDIC FIL-44-2008, OCC Bulletins 2013-29 and 2020-10.

Use of third parties does not diminish or remove banking organisations' responsibilities; principles apply to all third parties including fintechs; customer-facing activities can be critical activities; guidance creates no new requirements.

The 25 Jul 2024 joint statement identifies elevated operational, compliance, strategic, liquidity and concentration risks, consumer-protection risk, end-user confusion and misrepresentation of deposit insurance; companion RFI is OCC Bulletin 2024-21.

A secondary compilation lists 18 bank or holding-company actions tied to sponsor, fintech or third-party payments business from 8 Mar 2023 to 3 Sep 2026, seven terminated by Sep 2026; themes: TPRM, BSA/AML and CIP, prior approval of new partners.

Listed actions include Cross River (FDIC 8 Mar 2023), Blue Ridge (OCC 24 Jan 2024; terminated 13 Nov 2025), Lineage (FDIC 30 Jan 2024), Sutton (FDIC/Ohio 1 Feb 2024; CIP lookback within 120 days), Piermont (FDIC 27 Feb 2024), Thread (FDIC 21 May 2024; terminated 22 Dec 2025), Evolve (Fed/Arkansas 11 Jun 2024), Green Dot (Fed 19 Jul 2024), Hatch (FDIC 3 Apr 2025; terminated 21 Jan 2026), Community Federal Savings Bank (OCC 24 Apr 2026).
FDIC insurance protects against insured-bank failure, not middleware failure (secondary).
Revolut received a UK banking licence with restrictions in July 2024 and announced exit from mobilisation on 11 Mar 2026 (PRA approval), enabling FSCS-protected deposit accounts (secondary).
E-money is a claim on the EMI, not a deposit, so DGS cover does not apply; protection is safeguarding (EMD2 Art 7).
UK EMRs 2011 regs 33 to 34 cover distributors and agents and PSRs 2017 reg 34 covers agents; safeguarding in PSRs reg 23 and EMRs regs 20 to 24.

RBI Co-Lending Arrangements Directions 2025 (RBI/DOR/2025-26/139) issued 6 Aug 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026 (earlier adoption allowed); commercial banks excluding SFBs, LABs and RRBs, AIFIs and NBFCs incl. HFCs may co-lend.

Each partner retains at least 10% of each loan; funds routed through escrow; blended rate; originating lender DLG up to 5%; borrower-level asset classification; each share booked within 15 days of disbursement; charges in KFS; partnerships disclosed; LSP model remains under the Digital Lending Directions 2025.
CIP minimum information before opening: name, date of birth, address, identification number (TIN for US persons; passport or other government ID and country for non-US persons).

Verification within a reasonable time after opening by documents and/or non-documentary methods, with procedures for non-face-to-face opening and for lack of verification (when not to open, terms of use pending verification, when to close, when to file a SAR); list comparison; notice; reliance; records 5 years after closure.

Beneficial ownership: each individual owning 25% or more of equity plus one individual with significant control; certification at each new account; risk-based verification at least to CIP standards; exclusions; pooled vehicles and nonprofits control prong only; records 5 years.

Customer risk profile is required but there are no required categories; higher-risk customers need source of funds/wealth and more frequent review; no categorical requirement for periodic updates; event triggers include activity changes, ownership changes, red flags, law enforcement requests and negative media; CDD rule effective 11 Jul 2016, compliance 11 May 2018.

AMLR Art 52: beneficial ownership through ownership interest at 25% or more, direct or indirect, indirect holdings multiplied along chains and summed; by 10 Jul 2029 the Commission assesses lowering the threshold for higher-risk categories to a maximum of 15%.

FATF Digital ID guidance (6 Mar 2020) helps assess assurance levels of digital ID technology, architecture and governance for CDD, technology-neutral; Appendix D on assurance frameworks, Appendix E on US and EU frameworks; 1.7bn unbanked adults, 26% citing lack of documentation.
FFIEC lists biometrics, out-of-band devices, OTP devices and cryptographic keys as MFA factors and describes behavioural biometrics and device fingerprinting.
UK 2025 fraud: total losses GBP 1.28bn (up 4%); 4.06m cases (up 11%); GBP 1.68bn prevented; unauthorised GBP 703.4m (down 5%); APP GBP 576.4m (up 19%) (secondary on UK Finance).

UK 2025 APP: purchase, investment, romance and advance-fee scams GBP 437m (up 35%); investment GBP 221.5m (38%); advance fee GBP 58.4m; purchase scams 71% of cases; malicious redirection under a quarter of losses vs more than half in 2020; GBP 354.3m reimbursed (about 61%); 66% of cases originate online, 17% via telecoms (secondary).
From 7 Oct 2024 APP reimbursement up to GBP 85,000 per claim, split 50:50 between sending and receiving PSPs, on FPS and CHAPS; most reimbursed within five business days.

The 2021 guidance replaces the 2005 and 2011 internet banking authentication guidance, extends to employees, third parties and system-to-system access, requires periodic risk assessments and layered security, MFA or equivalent where needed; example controls and threats listed.

Banks report transactions of at least USD 5,000 where they know, suspect or have reason to suspect illegal-source funds, BSA evasion or no lawful purpose; file within 30 calendar days of initial detection, extendable 30 days if no suspect, never beyond 60; SAR confidentiality; 5-year retention.

CONC 5.2A requires creditworthiness assessment covering credit risk and affordability before entering or significantly increasing credit; reasonable steps on income and non-discretionary expenditure; unsupported income statements generally insufficient; proportionate; guarantees not counted for affordability.

SI 2025/859 (made 14 Jul 2025) sets Regulation Day 15 Jul 2026 for DPC; CONC 5.2A applies incl. DPC of GBP 50 or less; FOS only for agreements on or after Regulation Day; TPR window then six months to apply (secondary on CP25/23).
Final rules PS26/1 reported 11 Feb 2026, largely implementing CP25/23 with amendments; lending without permission or TPR after Regulation Day is a criminal offence (secondary).
CCD2 transposition by 20 Nov 2025, application from 20 Nov 2026, CCD1 repealed from 20 Nov 2026 (secondary).

CCD2 text: Art 2(2)(l) carves out agreements existing on 20 Nov 2026; APR defined in Art 3(7), calculated per Art 30 and Annex III; recitals cover interest-free BNPL, agreements up to EUR 100,000, ability and propensity to repay, no special-category or social-network data, human intervention for automated assessment, 30-day arrears notice, forbearance and debt advice.
APR determined by actuarial or US Rule method; accurate within 1/8 of 1 percentage point for regular and 1/4 for irregular transactions.

TILA exempts credit primarily for business, commercial or agricultural purposes and credit to non-natural persons; 1026.3(b) exempts credit above an annually CPI-adjusted threshold (not secured by dwelling, not private education loans).

Adverse action notice within 30 days after a completed application; 30 days after adverse action on an incomplete application or existing account; 90 days after an unaccepted counteroffer; written notice with specific reasons or right to reasons (request within 60 days, answer within 30).

Business credit: applicants with revenue of USD 1m or less may get oral or written notice and right to reasons at application; over USD 1m or trade credit/factoring: notice within a reasonable time, written reasons if requested within 60 days.

CFPB final rule published 22 Apr 2026, in force 21 Jul 2026, removes disparate-impact liability from Reg B, narrows discouragement and restricts for-profit SPCPs; 21 state AGs opposed; NYDFS says disparate impact may still be unlawful under state law; no reported change to 1002.9 (secondary).

Revised Section 1071 rule published 1 May 2026: data collection from 1 Jan 2028 with grace through 31 Dec 2028; threshold 1,000 covered originations in each of two prior years; small business revenue USD 1m or less; removed data points include application method, recipient, denial reasons, pricing, number of workers (secondary).

Reg F 'debt' means a consumer obligation primarily for personal, family or household purposes, so business-purpose debts fall outside Part 1006; creditors collecting own debts in own name are generally not debt collectors.
Call frequency presumption: no more than seven calls within seven consecutive days about a debt and none within seven days after a telephone conversation.

Closed-end retail charged off at 120 cumulative days past due, open-end at 180, by end of month; bankruptcy within 60 days of notice; fraud within 90 days of discovery; Substandard at 90 days; residential real estate valued by 180 days.

Open-end re-aging only if account at least 9 months old with 3 consecutive minimum payments, at most once in 12 months and twice in 5 years; closed-end extensions need explicit standards; no advances to pay interest; partial payments by 90% rule or aggregation, not both; NCUA did not adopt.
R01 Insufficient Funds is returned by the receiving bank within 2 banking days (vendor, secondary on Nacha).

Up to two reinitiations (three entries) within 180 days of the original effective date for R01/R09; R08 only with receiver authorisation; other reasons only after remedy; must match original company name, ID and amount (secondary).
Furnishers must have reasonable written accuracy and integrity policies, consider Appendix E guidelines and review periodically.
CDIA says furnishers must investigate CRA-referred disputes and correct, delete or verify within 30 or 45 days.

EBA describes redirection, decoupled and embedded approaches; redirection is not in itself an obstacle but can be if the only method and adds friction; obstacles include double SCA in PIS-only journeys without justification, manual IBAN entry in ASPSP domain, extra registration beyond eIDAS certificates and extra consent checks; 90-day reauthentication not itself an obstacle.
Delegated Regulation 2022/2360 adds a mandatory SCA exemption for AISP access (with conditions), limits Art 10 to direct access and extends renewal from 90 to 180 days (secondary).
The SCA amendments apply from 25 Jul 2023 (secondary).

FCA PS21/19 created Art 10A: ASPSPs may stop requiring reauthentication for TPP account information access; TPPs reconfirm explicit consent at least every 90 days; SCA on first connection; effective 26 Mar 2022, widespread adoption expected by 30 Sep 2022 (secondary).

CDR consent up to 12 months and only as long as reasonably needed; withdrawal at any time via dashboards; ADRs provide consent dashboards and data holders authorisation dashboards; withdrawal no harder than consent; data holders seek authorisation before disclosure; consumers can elect deletion of redundant data.

Resolucao Conjunta 7/2023 allows consent validity longer than 12 months and simplified renewal for individuals from Nov 2023; revocation at any time; direct institution-to-institution flow; BCB reported over 41.3m active consents for 27.2m customers (secondary).
UK OB v4.0, Brazil (profile v2.1.0) and Australia CDS build on FAPI 1.0 Advanced; FAPI 2.0 final 22 Feb 2025; CIBA Core 1.0 final 1 Sep 2021 (pointer to standards.md).
India AA has consent-and-data edges only, no value flow; Sahamati reported 2,880m+ accounts enabled and 1,970m+ consents raised (June 2026) (pointer to in.md).
Pending ledger entries may be archived if a transfer fails; corrections post reversing or difference entries (vendor).

SI 2021/716 creates payment institution and electronic money institution special administration as an alternative to liquidation/administration, entered by court order (regs 7 to 10), objectives and procedure regs 12 to 35, statement of proposals reg 37.

Three objectives: return relevant funds as soon as reasonably practicable; timely engagement with payment system operators, PSR, BoE, HMT and FCA; rescue or wind up; plus bar date, transfer mechanism, continuity of supply and FCA direction power; introduced 8 Jul 2021; Insolvency Rules effective 12 Nov 2021; FCA Dec 2020 consultation cited six insolvencies with only one returning funds (secondary).
The bank remains responsible for activities performed by third parties, so in a bank-partner model the bank is lender of record with Reg B and BSA obligations.
Reinsurance is a contract in which the cedent transfers part or all of its risk to a reinsurer; reinsurers can buy cover (retrocession); placed directly or through a broker.

US credit for reinsurance is governed by NAIC Model Law #785 and Model Regulation #786; licensed reinsurers need no collateral; non-US reinsurers generally post 100% unless Certified (reduced) or Reciprocal Jurisdiction (none).

The US-EU and US-UK Covered Agreements remove collateral and local presence requirements for qualifying reinsurers (own funds USD 250 million equivalent and 100% Solvency II SCR); all 56 US jurisdictions adopted the revisions by September 2022.

Case reserves are set for specific known claims; IBNR covers losses occurred but not reported (pure IBNR plus claims in transit); separate provision for development on known claims; reopened-claims reserves; LAE split allocated and unallocated (CAS 2021).

ACORD publishes P&C (XML, AL3), Life & Annuity XML (with DTCC EDI files), GRLC XML and JSON (claims, placing, accounting & settlement), Next-Generation Digital Standards for APIs and microservices, multi-functional and regional standards.

IRDAI health Master Circular (reported 30 May 2024): cashless authorisation immediately and within one hour; discharge within three hours; strive for 100% cashless; no documents from policyholders; no repudiation without claims review committee (secondary).

Also: 60-month moratorium; grace period 30 days (annual, half-yearly, quarterly) or 15 days (monthly); no renewal denial due to prior claims; TPAs paid with clawback; Rs 5,000 per day penalty if ombudsman award not implemented within 30 days (secondary).

RBI E-mandate Framework 2026 (RBI/DPSS/2026-27/396, issued and effective 21 Apr 2026) allows AFA-free recurring debits up to Rs 15,000 generally and Rs 1,00,000 for insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bills; pre-debit notification at least 24 hours; cards, PPIs and UPI; modify/withdraw/opt out with AFA.
Business Today (22 Apr 2026) reports the auto-pay rule changes consistently with the RBI framework (secondary).
From 15 Sep 2025 UPI P2M limits for insurance premiums and capital markets rose from Rs 2 lakh to Rs 5 lakh per transaction, up to Rs 10 lakh per day; P2P unchanged at Rs 1 lakh per day.
Bima Sugam Regulations 2024 notified 20 March 2024; operated by Bima Sugam India Federation; information hub live from 17 Sep 2025; Phase 1 and Phase 2 described as planned (secondary).
Full transactional go-live 'around November 2026' is attributed to media reports of IRDAI Chairman remarks; the article advises verifying with IRDAI.
India's 2025 amendments add managing general agents and insurance repositories to the intermediary definition; intermediary licences no longer need periodic renewal (annual fees instead) (secondary).
FSCS insurance protection for firms failed after 8 Oct 2020: 100% for compulsory, long-term, professional indemnity, death or incapacity and building guarantee policies; 90% for other insurance.

IFRS 17 measures groups of contracts at risk-adjusted present value of future cash flows plus a contractual service margin released as services are provided; onerous losses immediately; optional premium allocation approach.
IAIS adopted the ICS on 5 Dec 2024 (Cape Town) as a risk-based group-wide PCR for IAIGs and quantitative element of ComFrame; 59 IAIGs from 18 jurisdictions.

ICS timeline: 2025 methodology, 2026 baseline self-assessment, from 2027 jurisdictional assessments; ICP and ComFrame updates implemented from 2025; Nov 2024 assessment found the US Aggregation Method comparable with two convergence areas (interest rate risk, timing of supervisory intervention).

Directive (EU) 2025/2 of 27 Nov 2024 amends Solvency II on proportionality, supervision, reporting, long-term guarantees, macro-prudential tools, sustainability risks and group and cross-border supervision; entry into force 28 Jan 2025.
Published in the OJ on 8 Jan 2025; two years to transpose; applies at the latest from 30 Jan 2027 (secondary).
IDD dated 20 Jan 2016, published 2 Feb 2016, in force 22 Feb 2016.
Directive (EU) 2018/411 moved IDD application from 23 Feb 2018 to 1 Oct 2018 to allow Delegated Regulations 2017/2358 (POG) and 2017/2359 (IBIPs).

PRA PS15/24 (15 Nov 2024) restates Solvency II as PRA rules mostly effective 31 Dec 2024 (some items to 2025 and 2026); MA reform PS10/24 mostly from 30 Jun 2024; risk margin per SI 2024/1083; regime called Solvency UK.
Consumer Duty (PS22/9, 27 Jul 2022): effective 31 Jul 2023 for open products and 31 Jul 2024 for closed; four outcomes; cross-cutting rules; Consumer Principle.
FCA continues publishing Consumer Duty good-practice material (e.g. 10 Jul 2026 and 27 Jul 2026 reviews).

NAIC RBC: life formula adopted 1992 and implemented 1993; Model Act #312 (1993, revised 2012); #315 (1998, revised 2011); 300%+ no action; 200 to 300% trend test; below 200% graduated interventions; below 70% mandatory takeover.

The 2025 Act amends the Insurance Act 1938, LIC Act 1956 and IRDA Act 1999; assent 20 Dec 2025; in force 5 Feb 2026; FDI cap 74% to 100% (rules effective 30 Dec 2025; Press Note 1 (2026) of 9 Feb 2026) (secondary).

Foreign reinsurer branch net owned fund cut from INR 50bn to INR 10bn; IRDAI gains disgorgement and penalties up to INR 100m to a Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund; 'class of insurance business' defined for future composite licences (not yet created); Section 32A not yet notified (secondary).

RBC 2 took effect 31 Mar 2020 with the Insurance (Valuation and Capital) (Amendment) Regulations 2020 and MAS Notice 133, capturing more risks incl. catastrophe and operational, higher target confidence and clarified supervisory actions.

C-ROSS II: mandatory look-through, cost-basis for investment property, 100% charge on controlled non-insurance subsidiaries, stricter life future-profit recognition, full compliance no later than 2025 (secondary).
On 20 Dec 2024 the Financial Regulatory Administration extended the Solvency Supervision Rules (II) transition from end-2024 to end-2025 (secondary).
IFRS 17 applies to annual periods beginning on or after 1 Jan 2023, replacing IFRS 4 (2004); issued May 2017; amended June 2020.
BIS DvP Model 1 gross/gross trade by trade with simultaneous finality; Model 2 securities gross, funds net at end of cycle; Model 3 both net at end of cycle.
PFMI (published 16 Apr 2012) cover systemically important payment systems, CSDs, SSSs, CCPs and trade repositories.

NSCC CNS is CCP for nearly all US broker-to-broker trades in equities, corporate and municipal bonds and UITs; nets to one daily position per security per member; novation makes NSCC the counterparty once a trade passes validation; final instructions go to DTC; CNS credits or debits dividends and interest on open fails.
Q3 2026 CNS statistics: netting rate 98.6%, average margin requirements USD 18.3 billion.

DTC (1973) immobilises securities and makes book-entry ownership changes; Federal Reserve member, New York limited-purpose trust company and SEC-registered clearing agency; over 1.4 million active issues worth USD 87.1 trillion; end-of-day net settlement obligations.

Fedwire Securities provides issuance, maintenance and transfer of Treasury, agency, GSE and certain international organisation securities, mostly DvP with funds credited to master accounts, real time gross, final and irrevocable (OC 7); about 7,500 participants.
SEC Treasury clearing mandate deadlines: December 2026 (cash) and June 2027 (repo); FICC GSD Q2 2026 average daily activity USD 11.4 trillion; Sponsored and Agent Clearing models.

T2S exchanges cash and securities simultaneously, DvP in central bank money; 24 CSDs from 23 countries; EUR and DKK; dedicated cash account with a connected NCB plus CSD securities account; auto-collateralisation; Monday to Friday, closed on TARGET holidays.

CREST (operated by Euroclear UK & Ireland per BoE 2017) has offered real-time DvP since Nov 2001; BoE settles sterling in RTGS via CREST settlement bank accounts (zero overnight, funded each morning, swept back at day end) with irrevocable undertakings; high-frequency cycles; auto-collateralising repo; 20 settlement banks and about 17,000 members; DvP from 06:00, equity and gilt DvP ends 14:55.

India outright secondary G-sec trades settle T+1 via SGL securities and RBI current accounts on DvP-III; CCIL is CCP via novation, computes net obligations, sends settlement file to RBI, collects margins and maintains a Settlement Guarantee Fund; gilt holders via CSGL; repo first legs T+0 or T+1.
NDS-OM is an anonymous order-driven platform operated by CCIL for RBI; OTC trades reported within 15 minutes.

NSE Clearing describes itself as the largest CCP by exchange-traded derivatives contracts cleared in FY2024-25, maintains a Core Settlement Guarantee Fund and default waterfall, and publishes daily settlement statistics (e.g. 14 Oct 2026).

Rule 15c3-3: possession or control of fully paid and excess margin securities; Special Reserve Bank Account funded per Exhibit A; weekly computation by default, daily for average total credits of USD 500 million or more; separate PAB reserve account.
Rule 611 requires trading centres to maintain policies preventing trade-throughs of protected quotations, with exceptions incl. intermarket sweep orders.
UPI capital markets limit is Rs 5 lakh per transaction and Rs 10 lakh per day from 15 Sep 2025 (funding a broking or investment account).

SEC adopted T+1 on 15 Feb 2023 with compliance 28 May 2024; broker-dealers complete allocations, confirmations and affirmations by end of trade date; matching providers facilitate STP; advisers keep records.
Canada moved to T+1 on 27 May 2024 and the US on 28 May 2024 (secondary).

Regulation (EU) 2025/2075 of 8 Oct 2025 amends CSDR Art 5(2): trading-venue transactions settle no later than first business day after trading from 11 Oct 2027, with exemptions; OJ issue dated 14 Oct 2025.
UK T+1 go-live 11 Oct 2027; Taskforce plan 6 Feb 2025; government response 19 Feb 2025; FPC record 10 Apr 2025; efficiency target 28 May 2026; toolkit 25 Sep 2026; Q3 review 2 Oct 2026.
Wikipedia still describes the EU 11 Oct 2027 date only as an ESMA recommendation (Nov 2024) and India's T+1 as planned from 2022; superseded for the EU by Regulation (EU) 2025/2075.
CSDR Refit 2023/2845 of 13 Dec 2023, in force 16 Jan 2024, amends settlement discipline, cross-border services, supervisory cooperation, banking-type ancillary services and third-country CSDs.
EMIR 3 (2024/2987 of 27 Nov 2024, published 4 Dec 2024, in force 24 Dec 2024) aims to mitigate excessive exposure to third-country CCPs and improve EU clearing efficiency.

EMIR 3 active account requirement: counterparties over clearing thresholds in categories of substantial systemic importance; OTC IRDs in EUR and PLN and EUR STIR (not CDS); operationally functional account at an EU CCP; at least five trades per relevant subcategory per reference period (one for pension schemes).
MiFIR review 2024/791 of 28 Feb 2024, in force 28 Mar 2024: data transparency, consolidated tapes, trading obligations and ban on receiving payment for order flow.
ICSD 97/9/EC of 3 Mar 1997 entered into force 26 Mar 1997.

SIPC protects up to USD 500,000 per customer incl. USD 250,000 cash when a member fails and assets are missing; covers stocks, bonds, Treasuries, CDs, mutual funds and MMFs; not market losses, bad advice, most commodity futures, FX, unregistered investment contracts or unregistered digital assets; SIPC is not FDIC.
FSCS investments up to GBP 85,000 per person per firm (failures after 1 Apr 2019); deposits up to GBP 120,000 from 1 Dec 2025.
SEBI issued a circular on 1 Oct 2026 on display of investor awareness messages by stock brokers on apps and websites (Project Jagrook).
CSRC states aims including protecting investors, especially small investors.

DLT Pilot Regime 2022/858 of 30 May 2022, published 2 Jun 2022, in force 22 Jun 2022; defines DLT MTF, DLT SS and DLT TSS; instrument caps; aggregate EUR 6bn (transition at EUR 9bn); central bank money cash settlement by default, otherwise commercial bank money or e-money tokens; permissions up to six years; ESMA report after three years.

UK DSS is a live regulated environment operated by the BoE and FCA until 8 Jan 2029 unless extended; staged gates; equities, bonds, MMIs, fund units and emissions allowances in scope; derivatives and unbacked crypto out; page last updated 23 Dec 2024 names no admitted firms.
Project Guardian is a collaborative MAS-industry initiative testing asset tokenisation and DeFi feasibility with pilots in Singapore and elsewhere, plus policy work on rulebooks and governance.

Pontes links market DLT platforms and TARGET Services to settle DLT-based wholesale transactions in central bank money; initial launch 21 Sep 2026; cash tokens on the Eurosystem DLT platform or in T2 with final cash settlement in T2; DvP via Hash-Link; any entity with T2 access may participate.
